content: 1. Rapid HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) can provide same-day results and is recommended in antenatal care settings. This is particularly useful for pregnant women who present late in pregnancy, arrive in labor, or have not received their HIV test results prior to labor. 2. Before conducting the test, explain the procedure to the patient and obtain informed consent in accordance with national policies. 3. Use HIV test kits that are recommended by national or international health authorities, and strictly follow the manufacturer’s instructions for the selected rapid test. 4. Prepare a worksheet for documentation, label the test appropriately, and record the test batch number and expiration date. Ensure that the test kit has not expired. 5. Always wear gloves when drawing blood and adhere to standard safety precautions for waste disposal. 6. Inform the patient about the expected waiting time for the test results, whether they will be available on the same day or if a follow-up visit is required. 7. When drawing blood for multiple tests (e.g., hemoglobin, syphilis, and HIV), collect all samples at the same time. Use a sterile needle and syringe for venous blood collection or a lancet for a finger prick. 8. Perform the HIV test according to the manufacturer’s instructions and interpret the results as directed by the test kit guidelines: If the first test result is negative, no further testing is required. Record the result as HIV-negative. If the first test result is positive, conduct a second HIV rapid test using a different test kit. If the second test is also positive, record the result as HIV-positive. If the first test is positive but the second test is negative, repeat the testing process using a finger prick and both test kits. If both repeated tests are positive or both are negative, record the results accordingly. If the results remain discordant, use an alternative test or record the results as inconclusive. Advise the patient to return for repeat testing after two weeks or refer them to a hospital for confirmatory testing. 9. Ensure that the test results are communicated to the appropriate healthcare worker while maintaining strict confidentiality. 10. For umbilical cord care, use 1% chlorhexidine digluconate (delivering 4% chlorhexidine) in gel or liquid form as recommended. 11. When testing for proteinuria, provide the patient with a clean, labeled container and explain how to collect a clean-catch urine sample. Instruct the patient to: Clean the vulva with water. Spread the labia with fingers. Begin urinating freely, ensuring the urine does not dribble over the vulva. Collect the midstream portion of the urine in the container and remove the container before urination stops. 12. Analyze the urine sample for protein using either the dipstick method or the boiling method: For the dipstick method, dip the coated end of the dipstick into the urine sample, shake off excess urine, wait for the specified time, and compare the color change to the chart on the dipstick label. For the boiling method, boil the top half of the urine in a test tube. If the boiled portion becomes cloudy, add 2-3 drops of 2-3% acetic acid. Persistent cloudiness indicates the presence of protein, while clearing suggests no protein is present. 13. To check hemoglobin levels, draw blood using a sterile needle and syringe or a lancet, and follow the locally used method for analysis. 14. For malaria diagnosis, blood is typically obtained via a finger prick. The two common methods for diagnosis are light microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). The choice of method depends on local factors such as available skills, patient load, malaria epidemiology, and the potential for microscopy to diagnose other diseases. 15. When performing a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test for syphilis: Obtain informed consent and explain the procedure. Draw 5 mL of venous blood using a sterile needle and syringe, and place it in a clean test tube. Allow the blood to sit for 20 minutes to separate the serum, or centrifuge it for 3-5 minutes at 2000–3000 rpm. Use a pipette to withdraw serum, avoiding red blood cells, and place one drop (50 µL) of serum onto a test card circle. Spread the serum evenly using a clean spreader. Add one drop (20 µL) of antigen to the serum sample using a syringe with a dispensing needle. Do not stir. Rotate the test card for 8 minutes and inspect for clumping under good lighting. Compare results to the control circles on the card: Non-reactive (no clumping or slight roughness): Negative for syphilis. Reactive (visible clumping): Positive for syphilis. Weakly reactive (minimal clumping): Positive for syphilis, though weakly reactive results may require further confirmation. 16. During pregnancy, visit a healthcare provider as early as possible and attend at least four antenatal visits, even if no problems arise. The healthcare provider will monitor your health, help you create a birth plan, and provide necessary treatments and immunizations. 17. Take care of yourself during pregnancy by eating a healthy diet, taking prescribed supplements, resting, avoiding heavy lifting, and sleeping under an insecticide-treated bed net. Avoid alcohol, smoking, and unprescribed medications. Use condoms during sexual activity if there is a risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) or HIV. 18. Prepare a birth and emergency plan with your healthcare provider. Decide on the place of delivery, identify a skilled birth attendant, and organize necessary supplies. Plan for transportation and costs in case of emergencies. 19. After childbirth, continue eating a nutritious diet, taking iron supplements, resting, and drinking plenty of clean water. Maintain hygiene, especially in the perineal area, and use condoms if there is a risk of STIs or HIV. Attend routine postnatal check-ups, starting within 24 hours after delivery. 20. Be aware of danger signs during pregnancy and labor, such as vaginal bleeding, severe headaches, convulsions, fever, or difficulty breathing. Seek immediate medical care if any of these signs occur.
